extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars interested in philosophy of humor and Henri Bergson's theory of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Bergson's criteria for what makes situations, gestures, or individuals comic as presented in his 1900 essay Laughter (Le Rire). Focuses on the philosophical principles and 'laws' Bergson proposes about laughter and the comic's social role.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic is strictly a human phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson: "the comic is strictly a human phenomenon. A landscape cannot be a source of laughter, and when humans make fun of animals, it is often because they recognize some human behaviour in them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor presupposes recognition of human behavior; objects or non-human phenomena are not intrinsically comic except insofar as we attribute human qualities to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter requires indifference or detachment from sensibility and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: "laughter requires an indifference, a detachment from sensibility and emotion: it is more difficult to laugh when one is fully aware of the seriousness of a situation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional engagement reduces comedic response; a comic effect depends on a certain intellectual distance or lack of empathetic absorption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is primarily a collective/social phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is difficult to laugh alone, and it is easier to laugh collectively. One who is excluded from a group of people does not laugh with them; there is often a complicity in laughter. Thus, the comic is not a mere pleasure of the intellect, it is a human and social activity; it has a social meaning."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social context and complicity amplify comic effects; laughter functions within group dynamics rather than purely private cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: The source of the comic is rigidity or mechanism applied to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson locates the central cause of the comic in "mechanism inserted into life" — situations where movement, flexibility, or agility is replaced by rigidity or machine-like behavior (e.g., a man falling, absent‑mindedness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life is defined by perpetual movement; the comic arises when behaviour or character exhibits inflexibility, repetition, or mechanical traits instead of adaptable, living movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter serves a moral/social corrective role (punishment of inflexibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson: laughter makes people conscious of their vices and is "a factor of uniformity of behaviors... laughter is the punishment" that tends to eliminate ludicrous and eccentric attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond amusement, laughter functions to enforce social norms by highlighting and discouraging inflexible or eccentric conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: To laugh at ugliness requires a naive, immediate attitude and focus on a specific feature
rubrics_metrics.description: "Laughter can be caused by ugliness, but ugliness is not always comic. To laugh about ugliness, we need to have a naive, immediate, original approach, not to think. We also have to focus on a specific feature of the person and to associate the person with this feature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect from ugliness depends on immediate perception and the imaginative association of the person with an exaggerated trait (as cartoonists do), not on abstract aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures and movements are comic when they suggest machine-like mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: "Attitudes, gestures and movements of the human body are subject to laughter precisely in the way that body makes us think to a simple machine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conspicuous repetition, mechanical unconscious movements, parody and imitation (which reproduce the most mechanical aspects of a person) produce comic effect; repetition and complete similarity signal mechanism and provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituation can hide comic qualities (things comic de jure vs de facto)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Bergson's laws: "a lot of things are comic en droit (de jure) whereas they are not comic en fait (de facto), because common use and collective habits generalize these comic situations. Hence the mind needs to break with fashion to revive and to note the comedy of the situation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom and fashion desensitize audiences to potential comic features (e.g., fashionable clothes do not make us laugh because we are used to them); perceiving the comic may require dishabituation or a change of perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effect arises when attention is diverted from the mind to the physical body
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson: "is comic any incident which attracts our attention on the physique of a person while the mind is active" — the soul is flexible and active, the body is material and resistant; when attention shifts to the body's materiality the situation becomes comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrast between an active, flexible mind and a heavy, inflexible body (or when the body's material demands interrupt the mind) generates comic impression; the comic often depends on perceiving the body as burdening or obstructing the soul's activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: We laugh when someone appears as a material thing (person-as-thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: "we laugh every time somebody looks like a material thing, every time we are under the impression that someone is a thing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing a person as object-like or thing-like — devoid of the expected vivacity of life — produces comic effect; this ties into the broader theme of mechanism and material rigidity producing laughter.
